en: Now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman.
(1.1.1) Because [Brahman] is the source of the origin, etc., of this [world].
(1.1.2) Because [Brahman] has the scripture as its source. (1.1.3)

But that [Brahman is the cause], because of the concordance [of the texts]. (1.1.4) [The Self is the cause] because of the act of seeing; it is not something not based on scripture. (1.1.5) If it is argued that [the term "Self"] is secondary, we say no, because of the word "Self. (1.1.6)
Because liberation is taught for one who is intent upon that; because there is no statement regarding [the self] as something to be abandoned;
and because of its merging during deep sleep.
Because of the commonality of destination;
because it is so stated [in scripture];
and because of the repetition [of the term "consisting of bliss"].
If it be argued that [the Self] is not [Brahman] because of the word "modification," we say no, because of abundance;
and because its cause is designated;
and because it is celebrated as being exactly what is described in the words of the mantra.
Not the other, because it is not possible;
and because there is a designation of difference;
and because of desire, there is no dependence on inference.
And [the scripture] teaches his connection with this [body] in this [state];
(BBs 1.1.19) because there is instruction regarding those qualities within;
(BBs 1.1.20) and because there is a designation of difference, he is other [than the body]. (BBs 1.1.21)
It is space, because of its characteristic mark;
for this very reason, it is breath;
[it is] light, because of the mention of its feet.

If it be argued that [Brahman is not the subject] because of the mention of *chandas* (the Veda), we say no; for there is a statement regarding the fixing of the mind [on Brahman], and such is indeed seen [in scripture].
(BBs 1.1.25) And because the designation of the quarters as "the Real" (*bhūta*) and so forth is thus appropriate.
(BBs 1.1.26) If it be argued that it is not so because of the difference in instruction, we say no; for there is no contradiction in either case. (BBs 1.1.27)
"Likewise, [the Self] is the vital breath (prāṇa) because it follows after it.

If it be argued that this is not so because of the instruction regarding the speaker's own Self, [we reply: for in this [passage], there is an abundance of internal connection. But the instruction is given from the perspective of the scripture, as in the case of Vāmadeva."

If it be argued that [the Self within the lotus of the heart] is not Brahman because of the marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), we say no; because of the threefold nature of meditation, because [meditation on Brahman] has been resorted to elsewhere, and because such association is possible here;
because of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere;
and because the qualities intended to be expressed are appropriate. 1.1.31–1.2.2.
But it is not the embodied soul, because of the impossibility [of its being the agent];
and because of the designation of action and agent;
and because of the distinction of the word.
"And because of the Smṛti. [Objection:
"If it be argued that it is not so, because of its smallness and because of the designation of it as such, we say: no, because it is to be perceived as such, and because it is like space.
[Objection: "If it be argued that there would be the attainment of enjoyment [of pleasure and pain], we say: no, because of the difference in nature."
The Self [is meant], because of the inclusion of both the moving and the non-moving;
and because of the context;
for it is seen that "the two Selves have entered the cave."
And because of the qualification;
because of birth in the intermediate state;
and because of the designation of abodes and so forth.
And because of the mention of one distinguished by bliss (sukha),
and because of the mention of the path for those who have heard the Upaniṣads;
and because of non-abiding and impossibility, it is not the other.
The Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) [is the Lord] with respect to the deities, the worlds, and so forth, because His attributes are designated therein;
nor is He the one mentioned in the Smṛti, because attributes not belonging to that [Smṛti entity] are described;
for both [schools] study Him as distinct from the body.
[The Self taught here] possesses qualities such as invisibility, because of the statement of its attributes;
and because of the designation of distinctive attributes and difference, it is neither of the other two;
and also because of the presentation of its form.
Vaiśvānara [is the Self] because of the specific common term;
[this is] an inference based on what is remembered in the scriptures.

If it is argued that it is not so because of the word and other reasons, and because of his abiding within, we say no, because there is instruction for such a vision, because [the qualities] are impossible [in any other], and because they also study him as the Puruṣa.
For this very reason, [the Self] is neither a deity nor an elemental being.
Jaimini maintains that there is no contradiction even if [the Self] is perceived directly. Āśmarathya holds that [the Self is perceived] through manifestation.
Bādari [holds that the soul goes] by means of remembrance;
Jaimini [holds that it goes] by means of attainment, for scripture shows it thus;
and they record him in this [state].
The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word;
and because of the designation of that which is to be approached by the liberated;
and there is no inference [of another cause], because there is no word for that.
And [it is] the individual soul (prāṇabhṛt),
because of the designation of difference, because of the context, and because of the subject matter.
And on account of abiding and eating;
because of the teaching that the Plenum is superior to the serene being;
and because of the suitability of its attributes.
The Imperishable [is Brahman], because it supports everything up to the ether;
and that [supporting] is due to its command;
and because of the exclusion of any other state.
"He is [Brahman], because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of seeing" (BBs 1.3.13). "The small [ether] is [Brahman], on account of the subsequent [arguments]" (BBs 1.3.14).
"On account of the movement and the word; for thus it is seen, and there is an indicative mark" (BBs 1.3.15).
Because of the perception of this greatness of steadfastness in him;
and because of its well-known status. If it be argued that "He" refers to the other [the individual soul], we say no, because of impossibility.
If it be argued that [the Self] manifests its true nature from the north, [we reply:
but the reference has another purpose;
if it be argued on account of the mention of smallness, that has already been explained.
And because of the imitation of that;
furthermore, it is recorded in the Smṛti;
[the Self] is known from the Word alone.
But [the qualification for knowledge] depends on the heart, because the human race is the primary subject;

(Sūtra 25) Bādarāyaṇa holds that it extends even above that, because it is possible; (Sūtra 26) if it be argued that there is a contradiction regarding ritual action, we say no, because we observe the attainment of various states. (Sūtra 27)
If it is argued that [the world] is sound, we say no; because it originates from this [Brahman], as established by both perception and inference.
And for this very reason, its eternity is maintained.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction even in the recurrence [of creation], because names and forms are the same, as seen from scripture and tradition.
Jaimini [holds that there is] no entitlement [to knowledge] for those such as the Madhukas, because of the impossibility [of their possessing it];
and because [the sun] exists in the light [of the sun].
But Bādarāyaṇa [maintains] its existence, for it indeed exists.
For it is indicated by the mention of his disrespect toward Śuka and by his subsequent devotion to him;
and because of the attainment of the status of a Kṣatriya later on, as evidenced by the sign of Caitraratha;
and because of the reference to the initiatory rites and the statement of their absence [in the case of the other].
And because activity proceeds from the determination of its absence;
because of the prohibition of hearing, studying, and [understanding] the meaning; and because of the traditional teaching (smṛti);
and because of trembling.
Because of the perception of light;
because of the designation [of ether] as being a different entity and so forth;
and because of the distinction [between the Self and ether] in deep sleep and at the time of departure.
[The Self is] from words such as "husband" and so forth.

If it be argued that for some [it is] even inferential (ānumānika), we say no; because [the scripture] shows that it is grasped as presented through the metaphor of the body, and because it demonstrates this.
But it is subtle, because it is worthy of that [subtlety].
Because it is dependent on that, it is meaningful;
and because there is no statement that it is an object of knowledge.
If it is argued that [the scripture] does speak [of it], we say no, for the wise one [is not the speaker] according to the context.
And there is the presentation and the question regarding these three alone;
and [the term] "the Great" [is used];
and it is like the cups, because there is no distinction.
"But [the soul] has light as its starting point, for thus it is studied by some;
and because of the instruction of a mental construction, there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and so forth.
"Nor [is there a contradiction] even because of the inclusion of the number [five], owing to the diversity [of the elements] and because of the excess."
The vital breath and the others [are the subject] because of the supplementary statement;
for some, light [is the subject] when food is absent;
and because it is taught as the cause in the case of ether and the rest, exactly as it was designated.
Because of the drawing together;
because of the world being denoted;
if it be argued that [the Brahman] is not [meant here] on account of the characteristics of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), that has already been explained.
Jaimini [holds that the passage] has another meaning, on account of both the question and the answer; and likewise some [hold this] because of the connection of the sentences.
Āśmarathya [holds it to be] a sign for the establishment of the initial proposition.
"Audulomi holds that [the soul] departs from its state of being in this manner;
Kāśakṛtsna holds that [it does not depart] because of its continued existence;
and [Brahman is] the material cause as well, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples."
And because of the teaching on covetousness;
and because both are explicitly mentioned;
and because of the self-creation through transformation.
For the womb (*yoni*) is indeed proclaimed [as the source].
By this, all [points] have been explained, have been explained.
(BBs 1.4.27–28) If it is argued that there would be the fault of leaving no room for *smṛti*, it is not so; because there would be the fault of leaving no room for other *smṛtis*. (BBs 2.1.1)
And because the others are not perceived. (BBs 2.1.2) By this, Yoga is refuted.
(BBs 2.1.3) It is not so, because this [world] is of a different nature, and because that [nature] is known from scripture. (BBs 2.1.4)
"But there is a designation based on the presiding deity, because of distinction and because of following after;
for it is seen [in scripture].
But if it be said that [the effect] is non-existent, we say no, because [the text] is a mere negation."
"In dissolution, it would follow that [the world] is likewise [unreal]; therefore, [your position] is inconsistent.
But this is not so, because of the existence of examples, and because of the defects in your own position."

If it is argued that because reasoning is not firmly established, the object of inference must be otherwise [than as previously stated], even so, there follows the undesirable consequence of an absence of liberation (*anirmokṣa*).
By this, those [theories] not accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭāparigraha*) are also explained.
If it is argued that there would be no distinction [between the individual soul and Brahman] due to the soul's becoming one with the enjoyer, [we reply: it would be as in the world.
The non-difference of that [effect] from its cause is established on account of the words concerning "origin" (ārambhaṇa) and so forth;
because [the effect] is perceived when the cause exists;
and because of the existence of the other [the cause].

If it is argued that [the self] does not exist because of the designation of its non-existence, we say no; for there is a remainder of the statement [indicating it exists] through another attribute (BBs 2.1.17).
This is established by reasoning and by another scriptural term (BBs 2.1.18), and it is like a cloth (BBs 2.1.19).

And as in the case of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth. (2.1.20) Because there is the designation of [the Self] as other [than the body], there would follow the defects of not performing what is beneficial and so on. (2.1.21) But [the Self is] greater, because of the instruction of difference. (2.1.22)
And its impossibility is like that of stones and other such things.
(BBs 2.1.23) If it is argued that it is not so because we see the collection [of materials], we say no; for it is like milk.
(BBs 2.1.24) And it is also like gods and others in the world. (BBs 2.1.25)
Either there would be the consequence of [the whole] being affected simultaneously, or else there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning its partlessness.
But [this is not so], because of the scripture; for the scripture is the root of [all] verbal knowledge.
Moreover, it is thus in the case of the Self, for [diverse powers] are indeed manifold within it.
And because of the defects in one's own position;
and [the Lord] is endowed with all [powers], for that is seen from scripture;
if it is argued that this is not so because of the absence of organs, that has already been answered.
[The Lord acts] not because He has a purpose [to fulfill],
for [His activity] is mere sport, as in the world;
nor does He possess partiality or cruelty, because He is dependent [on other factors], for thus Scripture shows.
If it is argued that [the distinction between karma and its fruit] does not exist because there is no differentiation of karma, we say no, because [karma] is beginningless.
Furthermore, [the existence of karma] is both logically established and empirically perceived.
Moreover, all phenomena are logically established [as having causes].
And because the formation [of the world] is not possible, there is no inference [of a creator];
and because of the activity [of the world]. If it is argued that it is like milk or water, then that too must be addressed.
And because there is no stability in their distinction, and because they are independent;
and because [the effect] does not exist elsewhere, it is not like grass and so forth;
and even if [the cause] were admitted, the object would not exist.
If it is argued that it is like a person and a stone, even so: because of the impossibility of [the self] being the principal factor;
and because, if inferred otherwise, there would be a lack of the capacity for cognition.
And because of contradiction, [the theory] is inconsistent.
(BBs 2.2.10) Or, like the "large" and the "long" [arising] from the "short" and the "circular," (BBs 2.2.11) in neither case is there action; therefore, that [action] does not exist. (BBs 2.2.12)
And because of the admission of inherence (samavāya), there would be an infinite regress due to its similarity [to other relations];
and because it exists eternally;
and because of its possessing color and other qualities, the opposite [of what is claimed] is observed.
Because there are faults in both cases;
because of non-appropriation, there is absolute lack of dependence;
and even if the collection were caused by both, that [result] would not be attained.
If it is argued that [the self exists] because of mutual conditionality, we say no, because [the elements] are merely the causes for the arising [of subsequent moments].
Furthermore, because the preceding ceases when the succeeding arises;
otherwise, if this were not so, there would be a contradiction of your own thesis or simultaneity.
The non-attainment of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) [is not possible] because there would be no interruption [of the continuum],
because there would be faults in both cases,
and because there would be no distinction from space (*ākāśa*).
And because of recollection;
because that which is non-existent has never been seen;
and because, if this were so, even those who are indifferent would achieve [their goals].
It is not non-existent, because it is perceived;
and because of its difference in nature, it is not like a dream and so forth;
nor is it existent, because it is not [ultimately] perceived.
And because of momentariness;
and because it is impossible in every way;
and because [the characteristics] cannot exist in a single [entity].
And thus, the self would be non-omnipresent (2.2.34).
Nor is there a lack of contradiction even through modification, because of the objections regarding transformation and so forth (2.2.35).
Furthermore, there is no distinction [between the states] because both are eternal and because the final state remains constant (2.2.36).
Because of the inconsistency of a master;
because of the impossibility of a relationship;
and because of the impossibility of a presiding presence.
If it is argued that [the soul] is like an instrument, no; because of [the necessity of] experience and so forth.
[The soul would be] finite or non-omniscient.
Because of the impossibility of its origination.
And there is no instrument for an agent;
or, if [the self] exists as consciousness and so forth, there is no negation of that;
and because of contradiction.
Space does not exist [as a substance], because it is not mentioned [in the context of the elements];
however, it does exist,
because a figurative application [of the term] is impossible.
And because of the word [of scripture];
and there may be [the same designation] for one [thing], as in the case of the word "Brahman";
there would be a loss of the proposition because of the non-difference from the words.
But as far as there is modification, there is division, as in the world;
by this, the wind is explained.
But the non-existence of the existent is impossible, because it is not logically established.
Therefore, it is fire; for thus he says:
"Water" (BBs 2.3.11);
"Earth," because of the context, the form, and other words (BBs 2.3.12).
But he [the self] emerges from that very contemplation because of its characteristic mark;
however, the sequence is established as the reverse of this.

If it is argued that consciousness and the mind arise in sequence between [the elements] because of their characteristic marks, we say no, because there is no distinction [in the application of the rule].
But the designation [of the Self] as being dependent on the moving and the non-moving is figurative, because it exists only when those [bodies] exist.
(2.3.16) The Self [is not born], because of scripture and because of its eternity according to those [scriptures]. (2.3.17) Therefore, it is indeed a knower. (2.3.18)
[The soul is not atomic] because of [the scriptural mention of] its departure, going, and returning;
and because of the two subsequent [statements] regarding its own self.
If it be argued that it is not atomic because of a scriptural statement to that effect, we say no, because of the context of the other [passage].
And [the soul is all-pervading] because of its own specific term and because of measurement.
There is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood.
If it is argued that there is a distinction in its location, we say no, because it is accepted [to be present] in the heart.
Or [the relationship is] due to the quality, as in the world;
there is a distinction, as with fragrance;
and thus it is shown.
Because it is taught separately [from the Self].
(BBs 2.3.28) But its designation by that [name] is due to its having those qualities as its essence, as in the case of the wise man.
(BBs 2.3.29) And because it persists as long as the existence of the body, there is no fault, since it is seen to be so. (BBs 2.3.30)
But because it exists [already] and is subject to manifestation, like masculinity and so forth;
otherwise, there would follow either its eternal perception or non-perception, or else a restriction to one or the other.
[The Self is] an agent, because the scriptures have a purpose.
Because of the teaching on the abidings (vihāra),
because of appropriation (upādāna),
and because of designation (vyapadeśa) in action— if there were not a reversal of the description [of the agent]. (BBs 2.3.34–36)
There is no fixed rule, just as in the case of perception;
because of the reversal of capacity;
and because of the absence of meditative concentration.
And as the carpenter [acts] in both ways;
but [the soul acts] from another, because that is heard [in scripture];
but [the Lord] has regard for the effort made by the soul, because otherwise the injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered meaningless, and so forth.
He is a part [of Brahman], because of the designation of difference, and also because otherwise [he is designated as one]; for some record him as being a fisherman, a woodcutter, and so forth.
This is also from the wording of a mantra, and it is likewise recorded in Smṛti.
The Supreme is not like that, as in the case of light and so forth;
and they remember [this] as well.
Permission and avoidance [of actions apply to the soul] due to its connection with the body, as in the case of light and so forth.
And because there is no continuity, there is no confusion [of cognitions];
and it is merely an appearance,
because there is no restriction regarding the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
And the same applies to the intentional meanings (*abhisandhi*) and so forth.
(BBs 2.3.52) If it is argued that [the whole is perceived] because of its location in a part (*pradeśa*), we say no, because [the part] is included within [the whole].
(BBs 2.3.53) Likewise, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). (BBs 2.4.1)
Because a secondary sense is impossible;
because it is heard before that [mind];
and because speech is preceded by that [mind].

And because the seven [bases] are specified as being distinct from the course [of rebirth], whereas the hands and so forth exist while that course persists; therefore, it is not so. Furthermore, they are subtle.
And it is the most excellent.

(BBs 2.4.8) It is not merely the function of air, because it is taught separately. (BBs 2.4.9) But it is like the eye and other organs, because of its being taught together with them and for other reasons. (BBs 2.4.10)
And because it does not act [independently], there is no fault; for it shows this:
"It is designated as having five functions, like the mind;
and it is atomic. (BBs 2.4.11–13)
But the presiding over fire and the other elements belongs to Him, because of the scriptural teaching;
because [He is] like the vital breath (prāṇa), according to the sacred word;
and because of His eternity.
Those [faculties] are the senses (indriyas), because they are designated as such, except for the "best" one;
because of the scriptural mention of their distinction;
and because of their difference in nature.
But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who makes the triplication, because of the scriptural instruction;
meat and so forth consist of earth, according to the literal statement, as do the other two elements.
But on account of their predominance, there is that designation; indeed, there is that designation.
In the interval between death and rebirth, he goes enveloped [by the subtle elements], as established by the questions and the answers;
because [the soul] consists of three [qualities]; because of the predominance [of one quality over the others];
and because of the departure of the vital breaths.
If it be argued that [the souls do not go by the path of the gods] because of the scriptural mention of the destination of Agni and others, we say no, because that is figurative (BBs 3.1.4).

If it be argued that [they do not go] because they are not mentioned in the first [section], we say no, for it is precisely those [souls] who are intended, as this is logically consistent (BBs 3.1.5).

If it be argued that [they do not go] because they are not explicitly mentioned [there], we say no, because those who perform sacrifices and other works are understood [to be the subject] (BBs 3.1.6).
Or it is figurative because they do not know the Self; for scripture shows this.
"Upon the exhaustion of their work, those possessing residual karma [return], according to scriptural vision and traditional teaching, in the same manner and otherwise.
If it be argued that this is due to conduct, Kārṣṇājini says it is for the purpose of indication.
"If it is argued that [the passage] is meaningless, we say no, because it depends on that;
however, Bādari holds that it refers only to good and evil deeds;
moreover, it is heard in scripture regarding those who perform undesirable acts and so forth."
But in the case of the Saṃyamaṇa [hell], there is the ascent and descent of others after they have experienced [the results of their karma], because their course is observed;
and they remember it;
moreover, there are seven.

And even in that case, there is no contradiction because of its operation [therein]. (BBs 3.1.16) But it is because "knowledge and action" are the subjects under discussion. (BBs 3.1.17) It is not so in the third case, because it is not perceived as such. (BBs 3.1.18)
Moreover, it is recorded in the world;
and because of observation [of the cause];
the third term includes that which arises from grief.
There is an attainment of the state of being [of that nature], because of the logical possibility;
not after a very long time, because of the specific distinction;
[this is so] because of the mention [of the souls] as before in the case of those presided over by others.
If it be argued that [the soul] is impure, we say no, because of the scriptural statement;
furthermore, there is the connection with the seed-discharger,
and from the womb comes the body.
The creation occurs in the intermediate state (saṃdhye), for so the scripture says;
and some say that the creator is the father and others [the sons];
but it is mere illusion (māyāmātra), because its true nature is not fully manifested.
For this is indicated by scripture, and those who know it declare it so:
"But [the Self] is concealed by meditation on what is other than itself; for from that come its bondage and its opposite (liberation).
Or rather, even that [concealment] is due to connection with the body. (Brahma Sūtra 3.2.4–6)
The absence [of that dream experience] occurs in the channels and in the Self, according to scriptural statements;
therefore, awakening arises from this [Self].
But it is that very same [Self] [that awakens], on account of action, recollection, scriptural words, and injunctions.
O simple one, the state of "half-attainment" follows by elimination.
(3.2.10) The Supreme does not possess both characteristics even from the perspective of its locations, for it is so everywhere.
(3.2.11) If it be argued that this is not so because of difference, we say no; for there is no such statement regarding each [location] individually. (3.2.12)
Moreover, some hold this view:
for that [form] is indeed like formlessness because it has that as its primary nature;
and it is like light because it is not purposeless.
And it says "only that" (tanmātra);
furthermore, it is shown and also remembered;
for this very reason, there is a comparison with the reflection of the sun and so forth.
"But because it is not grasped like water, it is not so;

[the reflection] possesses increase and decrease because it is included within [the mirror], and thus there is consistency with both [the mirror and the object]; and because it is so observed. (BBs 3.2.19–21)
For [the scripture] denies that the Self is limited to what has been previously described, and then declares further about it;
for it says that it is unmanifest.
Moreover, it is perceived through direct intuition and inference when one is in a state of complete devotion.
And there is non-distinction [of the Lord] from light and so forth, and light [is manifested] through practice in action;
therefore, [the Lord is] eternal, for such is the mark.
But because of the designation of both, [He is] like a serpent and its coil.
Or, it is like light and its substratum, because it possesses the nature of luminosity (tejastva);
or as before;
and because of the refutation.
[The Lord is] superior [to the individual soul], because of the designations of a bridge, measurement, connection, and distinction (BBs 3.2.31).
But on account of similarity,
[the designation of difference] is for the sake of the intellect, as in the case of the "feet" (BBs 3.2.32–33).
Because of the distinction of location, as in the case of light and so forth;
because of logical consistency;
and likewise because of the negation of others.
By this [sūtra], its omnipresence is established on account of the words "extent" (āyāma) and so forth;
the fruit [arises] from that [Brahman] because it is logical;
and because it is so stated in scripture.
Jaimini [holds that meditation is] dharma for this very reason;
but Bādarāyaṇa holds the former view because of the mention of a cause.
[The knowledge of Brahman] is recognized through all Vedāntas because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth.
If it is argued that [the rule] does not apply because of differences [in the texts], we say no, for even in the case of a single [text], it is so;

because of the qualification in the *Samācāra* [Smṛti] regarding the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*), and because of the restriction being like that of the *Sava* sacrifice; and the scripture also shows this.
There is a synthesis [of the two meditations] because there is no difference in their meaning, as in the case of supplementary injunctions regarding what is common.
If it be argued that there is a difference because of the word, we say no, because there is no distinction.
Or rather, there is no synthesis because of the difference in context, as in the case of the "higher than the high" (parovarīyas) and other such passages.
If it is argued that [the objection] is based on a mere designation, it has already been stated that such a thing does exist;
(BBs 3.3.8) because of pervasion, [the argument] is consistent; (BBs 3.3.9) and because there is no difference among all [things], these others are likewise [included]. (BBs 3.3.10)
Bliss and the other qualities belong to the Principal [Brahman].
(BBs 3.3.11) The possession of "joy as the head" and so forth is not attained [in all texts], for increase and decrease occur only where there is difference.
(BBs 3.3.12) But the others [the qualities] are present everywhere because their meaning is common. (BBs 3.3.13)
Because there is no purpose for meditation [on the individual soul];
because of the word "Self";
and because the grasping of the Self [occurs] as in other cases, on account of what follows.
If it is argued that [the self exists] because of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), it would follow from the restriction [of the scripture].
(BBs 3.3.17) Because of the explanation of the effect, there is something not previously known (*apūrva*).
(BBs 3.3.18) And likewise, because there is no difference in the case of what is common. (BBs 3.3.19)
Because of the connection, it is thus in other cases as well;
or rather, it is not so, because there is a distinction;
and [the scripture] also demonstrates this.
And because of the gathering [of materials], the heaven-reaching [sacrifice], and likewise from this;
because, as in the case of the Puruṣa-vidyā, the others are not mentioned;
and because of the difference in meaning, such as piercing and so forth.

But in the case of falling away [from a lower state], there is a transition [to a higher one] because the word for "approaching" (upāyana) is supplementary; as in the cases of the *kuśa* grass, the meters, the praise, and the singing. This has been stated [in the Sūtra].
(3.3.26) In the state after death (*sāmparāya*), there is no need to cross over [any obstacles], for so it is with others.
(3.3.27) It is according to one's will, since both [options] are not contradictory. (3.3.28)
The meaningfulness of the state [of rebirth] is established in both ways; otherwise, there would be a contradiction.
It is logical because its characteristic object is perceived, as is seen in the world.
There is no restriction for all [beings], as there is no contradiction with scripture and inference.
The persistence of those who hold office lasts as long as their term of office (BBs 3.3.32).

But there is a restriction of those who possess notions of the syllable [Om] based on its commonality and its specific nature, as in the case of the *aupasada* sacrifice; this has been stated (BBs 3.3.33).
Because of the declaration of this much [is all] (BBs 3.3.34).

If it is argued that [the self] is like the collection of living beings within [the body], and otherwise its distinction would be untenable, we say no; for it is like other instructions. Indeed, they distinguish [the self] through exchange, as in the case of others.
For those very [vows] consist of truth and so forth;
desire and so forth [are excluded] elsewhere than in those [specific cases], such as the bases (āyatana) and so on.
Due to reverence, there is no omission.
Because it is so stated when [the sacrifice] has arrived;

there is no restriction regarding the determination of that [result], because it is seen as such; and the fruit is an absence of obstruction, like the separate [performance of] offerings. This has been explained just like the case of the offering.
On account of the abundance of indicatory marks, that [meditation] is indeed more powerful; for that too,
the previous alternative would apply because of the context, as in the case of the mental [sacrifice],
and because of the extended application (atideśa).
But knowledge alone [is the means], because of the definitive determination;
and because it is seen [in scripture];
and because there is no sublation, since the authority of direct revelation (śruti) and other means is stronger.
On account of the connection and other factors, it is seen to be like the distinctness of other forms of wisdom; this has been stated [in the Sūtra].
(BBs 3.3.50) Even on account of similarity, there is no attainment of the world, because it is perceived to be like death.
(BBs 3.3.51) Furthermore, the nature of the word is such by virtue of what follows, for the connection exists due to abundance. (BBs 3.3.52)
[The soul is one] because it exists in the body as a single entity.
Its distinction [from the body] is due to its presence when the body is present; however, this is not like the case of perception.
But those [rites] connected with the limbs are not [to be performed] in all branches, for they are restricted to each Veda.
Or rather, there is no contradiction, as in the case of mantras and the like.
(BBs 3.3.56) The preeminence of the "Great" [Self] is like that of the sacrifice; for the scripture shows it to be so.
(BBs 3.3.57) Because of the difference in various words and so forth. (BBs 3.3.58)
The option exists because the fruit is not distinguished [from that of the obligatory rites].

(BBs 3.3.59) However, the optional rites may be combined according to one's desire, or they may not, because of the absence of the aforementioned reason. (BBs 3.3.60) Regarding the subsidiaries, their status is according to their respective bases. (BBs 3.3.61)
And because of the teaching of the learned;
because of the combination [of the qualities];
and because of the scriptural statement regarding the commonality of the qualities.
Or rather, it is not so, because their coexistence is not heard [in scripture],
and because [the contrary] is seen;
therefore, Bādarāyaṇa maintains that the human goal [is attained] from the Word.

Jaimini [holds] that because it is a subordinate element (*śeṣa*), it is a statement of human purpose (*puruṣārthavāda*), as in other cases; [this is so] because of the observation of [the Lord's] conduct, because of the scriptural statement to that effect,
and because of the Vedic revelation.
Because of the act of taking hold together;
because of the injunction for one who possesses that [quality];
and because of the restriction.
But because of the additional instruction, Bādarāyaṇa holds this view, for such is seen [in scripture].
(3.4.8) The vision, however, is equal. (3.4.9) It is not universal. (3.4.10)
The distribution is like that of a hundred [coins];
it belongs to one who possesses merely the study [of the Veda],
because there is no distinction [between them].
Or it is for the sake of praise, or it is consent; some say it is by way of acting according to one's own desire, and others say it is through suppression.
And [the practice] among those who have drawn up their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) is based on scripture;

for Jaimini holds that there is a reference [to them], since there is no injunction [for them] and scripture indeed censures such [a life]. Bādarāyaṇa holds that it is to be performed, because of the scriptural statement of equality.

Or rather, it is an injunction, like the rule regarding the holding [of the cup]. (BBs 3.4.20) If it is argued that this is merely a commendation because of its connection with another [injunction], we say no, because it conveys something not previously established (apūrva). (BBs 3.4.21) And because it is expressed by a word denoting an action (bhāva-śabda). (BBs 3.4.22)
If it is argued that [the Vedas] have only variable meanings, we say no, because they are specified [as having a fixed meaning];
likewise, because they are connected as a single coherent discourse;
and for this very reason, there is no dependence on firewood and such [external factors].
And there is a requirement for all [works], because of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse;
nevertheless, one should be endowed with tranquility, self-control, and the like, because those are enjoined as its (knowledge's) auxiliaries and must therefore necessarily be practiced.
Furthermore, there is no permission for all [forbidden acts] even in the event of the loss of life, because that is what is seen [in scripture].
And because there is no contradiction;
furthermore, it is recorded in the Smṛti;
and therefore, there is a scriptural injunction regarding the absence of acting according to one's own will.
And because it is prescribed, the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma) [are also to be performed];
and because they act as auxiliaries;
and in every way, those [same duties] [are required], on account of the two-fold scriptural indication.
And it demonstrates non-overpowering;
furthermore, because that is seen in the interval;
moreover, it is recorded in memory.
And there is a special favor [for the one who has entered the order]. (BBs 3.4.38) But for this reason, the other state is superior, also because of the indicative mark.

(BBs 3.4.39) But for one who has become that [state], there is no returning to what he was not; according to Jaimini as well, because of the restrictive rule and because of the absence of that form. (BBs 3.4.40)
Nor is it [a sin] pertaining to one holding an office, because of the inference of a fall [from that status] and because such [office-holding] is impossible for him.
However, some say that even a minor offense (*upapātaka*) is of the same nature as eating [forbidden food].
But outside [the community], it is both ways, according to the Smṛti and established custom.
"Because the fruit is declared for the master [of the sacrifice], so says Ātreya. The office of the officiating priest belongs to the sacrificer, so says Auḍulomi, for he is hired for that purpose.
And because of the scriptural statement."
There is an injunction for another auxiliary means in the third [stage], as in the case of one who possesses that [means], like the beginning of the injunction;
but the conclusion is made with the householder because of the totality [of duties] (BBs 3.4.47).
However, there is instruction for the others as well, just as for the vow of silence (mauna) (BBs 3.4.48–49).
Because it follows from the absence of manifestation;
because even in this life [the fruit arises] when there is no obstruction to what has been undertaken, as that is observed;
thus there is no fixed rule regarding the fruit of liberation, because that state is determined, because that state is determined.
There is repetition because of the frequent instruction;
and because of an indicative mark;
moreover, they acknowledge [the self] as "the Self" and cause others to grasp it as such.
Not in a symbol, for he is not that;
the vision of Brahman [is to be applied] to the subordinate members because of their excellence;
and the cognitions of Āditya and so forth are to be applied to the subordinate members because it is logical.
Because of its occurrence while seated;
because of meditation;
and with reference to immovability.
And they remember [the teaching]:
"Wherever there is one-pointedness of mind, [liberation occurs] there, without distinction" (BBs 4.1.10);
and "for it is seen even in that case until the final departure" (BBs 4.1.11–12).
Upon the realization of that [Truth], there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, because of the designation thereof.

(4.1.13) For the other as well, there is likewise non-clinging; however, at death [the remainder perishes]. (4.1.14) But only those prior [karmas] whose effects have not yet begun [perish], for that is the limit. (4.1.15)

But the Agnihotra and other such rites are for that very purpose [of liberation], because it is so seen in scripture. For some, there is another way for both [knowledge and action] as well; indeed, it is said: "Whatever one does with knowledge... and so forth.
But having exhausted the others through experience, he then attains [the state of union];
for speech is seen to merge into mind, because of the scriptural statement and because of the word [of the teacher].
And for this very reason, all [the organs] follow suit.
That mind [merges] into the vital breath, according to the subsequent [scriptural passage].
That [vital breath] [merges] into the presiding deity, because of its approaching that [deity] and other reasons.
[The vital breath merges] into the elements, because of the scriptural statement to that effect.
For [the scripture] does not show [the soul] in one [place];
and there is equality [of the soul's state] from the commencement of its departure until it reaches immortality without having burned away [its karma];
and because the designation of transmigratory existence continues until that absorption.
It is subtle by measure, because it is perceived in that way; therefore, it cannot be destroyed. And because this very [subtlety] is logically established, this is the "heat" (ūṣman).
If it be argued that [the soul is not the agent] because of a prohibition, we say no, because [the prohibition refers only to the] embodied [self].
For this is clear from some [scriptural passages],
and it is also recorded in traditional Smṛti.
Regarding those [other paths], it is so because it has been stated thus:
"There is no division, because of the scriptural statement" (BBs 4.2.15).

"Then there is the flaming of the tip of the heart-artery; its door is illuminated by that [light], through the power of knowledge, and by means of the application of the recollection of the path which is the remainder of that [knowledge]; favored by the one dwelling in the heart, [the soul departs] by means of the hundred-and-first [artery]" (BBs 4.2.17).

[The soul] follows the rays. If it is argued that this is not so at night, we say no; for the connection [between the soul and the rays] persists as long as the body exists, and scripture also demonstrates this.
Therefore, [the soul goes to Brahman] even during the southern course of the sun.
And these two [paths] are recorded in Smṛti with reference to yogins; for they are both based on Smṛti.

(BBs 4.2.21) [The soul travels] by way of the flame and so forth, because that is well-known from scripture. (BBs 4.3.1) [The soul goes] from the year to the air, on account of the distinction between the general and the specific. (BBs 4.3.2)
Varuṇa presides over lightning because of their connection;
[the deities are] conducting [souls], because of the indicative marks thereof;
this is established because of the delusion regarding both.
"By the lightning alone," because of the scriptural statement to that effect;
"the effected [Brahman]," according to Bādari, because the movement [of the soul] is possible toward it;
and "because of its being specified."
But that designation [of the soul] is due to its proximity;
(4.3.9) because when the effects have ceased, it is designated as being "beyond" [the world] together with its presiding overseer; (4.3.10) and because of Smṛti. (4.3.11)
But Jaimini [holds that it refers to Brahman] because of its primary meaning;
and because of scriptural evidence;
and because there is no intention to treat it as a mere ritual act.
Bādarāyaṇa maintains that [the Lord] leads those who do not rely on symbols, because there is a fault in both cases, and because of the nature of their resolve (tatkratu);
He also shows a distinction [between them].
And the manifestation [of the Self] occurs by its own [nature] upon reaching [the Supreme], because of the scriptural word.
The liberated one [is the self], because of the promise;
the self [is the subject], because of the context;
[it is so] because it is seen as non-distinct.
Jaimini [holds that the soul exists] in the state of Brahman, on account of the introductory statements and so forth;
Auḍulomi [holds that it exists] as mere consciousness, because its nature consists of that;
and Bādarāyaṇa [concludes] that even so, there is no contradiction because of the introductory statement and because of the prior existence [of the soul].
"But [the soul's power] is from mere volition alone, because of the scriptural statement";
"And for this very reason, it has no other master";
"Bādari declares its non-existence [in the absence of the body], for thus [the scripture] says."
Jaimini [holds that the sacrifice] has existence, because of the mention of its various forms;
therefore, Bādarāyaṇa [holds it to be] of both kinds, like the twelve-day sacrifice;
for in the absence of a body, it is possible as in the case of the twilight rites.
In the state of existence, it is like being awake;
for the scripture shows that the "entering" (āveśa) is like a lamp.
Indeed, it is made manifest as referring to either of the two: deep sleep (svāpyaya) or union (sampatti).
[The liberated soul] is excluded from the world-activity, because of the context and because [the soul] is not present [there].
(4.4.17) If it is argued that this is not so because of the direct scriptural teaching, we say no; for that teaching refers to one who resides within the circle of authority [of the cosmic office].
(4.4.18) And [the soul] abides in the realm of transformation, for the scripture thus declares its state. (4.4.19)
And thus he demonstrates perception and inference;
because of the mark of equality in mere enjoyment;
"no return, according to the scripture; no return, according to the scripture."
